title: CNN Fundamentals
blurb: Tests why convolutions beat fully connected layers on images, weight sharing as an inductive bias, equivariance against invariance, the output-size formula, kernel, stride and padding choices, the LeNet-AlexNet-VGG lineage, and when augmentation helps.

refLinks.label: §68.2.1 Weight Sharing as an Inductive Bias

questions.prompt: A 224 × 224 colour image feeds a fully connected layer with 1,000 hidden units. About how many weights is that, in millions? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 inputs, times 1,000 units = 150,528,000 weights, about 150.5 million, none shared.

questions.prompt: What assumption does a CNN build in that a fully connected layer doesn't?
options: Local patterns mean the same thing anywhere.
Objects always appear at the centre of the frame.
Every pixel is independent of its neighbours.
Colour matters more than shape for recognition.
questions.explanation: This is true of natural images, so building it in saves the network learning spatial structure from scratch with far more parameters.

refLinks.label: §68.2.1 Weight Sharing as an Inductive Bias

questions.prompt: A 3×3 convolution maps 16 input channels to 32 output channels, with a bias per output channel. How many parameters does it have?
questions.explanation: 3 × 3 × 16 × 32 = 4,608 weights, plus 32 biases, gives 4,640. The same weights apply at every position.

questions.prompt: Convolution alone is translation equivariant. What does that mean?
options: The kernel changes shape as it moves across the image.
If the input shifts, the feature map shifts with it.
If the input shifts, the output stays exactly the same.
The network ignores where features appear.
questions.explanation: Equivariant means "shifts with the input". Invariant means "doesn't change when the input shifts", which pooling moves the network toward.

questions.prompt: What does max-pooling add to a stack of convolutions?
options: It increases the spatial size of the feature map.
It learns which features to keep, like a strided convolution.
It drops exact position, toward invariance.
It adds weights that make the network equivariant.
questions.explanation: Pooling keeps the strongest response in a window and drops where it was. It is fixed, not learned, and it shrinks the map.

questions.prompt: Using conv_output_size, what is the output size for an 8-pixel input, a 3×3 kernel, no padding and stride 1?
questions.explanation: (8 + 0 − 3) // 1 + 1 = 6. Without padding, each layer shrinks the map by kernel_size − 1.

questions.prompt: A 32-pixel input passes through a 5×5 convolution with padding 2 and stride 2. What size comes out?
What padding keeps the size the same for a 7×7 kernel at stride 1?
What is the most common cause of a shape error on a new CNN's first forward pass, per Procedure 68.1?
options: A kernel size that isn't a power of two
Using ReLU after a pooling layer
Too many output channels in the last convolution
A wrong flatten size before the first FC layer
questions.explanation: Compute each layer's output size in sequence to get the flatten dimension right, rather than guessing.

questions.prompt: What does a strided convolution offer over max-pooling for downsampling?
options: It learns what to keep while it downsamples.
It needs no parameters at all.
It always keeps the spatial size unchanged.
It makes the network fully invariant in one step.
questions.explanation: Pooling is fixed. A stride-2 convolution downsamples and learns at once, which is why modern architectures lean that way.

questions.prompt: What was VGG's key design idea?
options: Stack many small 3×3 convolutions
Run several kernel sizes in parallel and concatenate them
Add skip connections around every pair of layers
Scale depth, width and resolution together
questions.explanation: Stacked small kernels grow the receptive field as well as large ones, with fewer parameters. Parallel kernels are Inception, skips are ResNet, and compound scaling is EfficientNet.

questions.prompt: Three stacked 3×3 convolutions cover the same receptive field as one 7×7. Per input-output channel pair, how many weights do the three 3×3 layers use, against 49 for the 7×7?
questions.explanation: 3 × 9 = 27 against 49. Stacking small kernels is cheaper for the same reach, which is the trade-off the chapter describes.

questions.prompt: What happens to a plain CNN pushed well past about 20 layers?
options: It gets worse even on the training set, from vanishing gradients.
It trains faster, since each layer has less to learn.
It overfits, scoring perfectly on training data but badly on test.
Nothing changes, since depth always adds capacity.
questions.explanation: Worse training accuracy rules out simple overfitting. Chapter 69's residual connections address it.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 68.3 leave out horizontal flips for digits?
options: Digits are always symmetric, so flips add nothing.
Flips are too expensive to compute on small images.
Flips only work on colour images.
A flipped digit can mean something else, or nothing.
questions.explanation: A flipped cat is still a cat, but a flipped 7 isn't a 7. Augmentations must preserve the label.

questions.prompt: Augmentation scored 0.866 ± 0.013 against 0.874 ± 0.016 without it. How does the chapter read that?
options: A bug in the augmentation code.
A clear harm, so augmentation should never be used.
No real gain. Shifts were too strong for 8×8.
A clear win, once the noise is accounted for.
questions.explanation: The gap is within noise. A "small" shift is a large fraction of an 8×8 image, so augmentation strength must fit the data's scale.

questions.prompt: How could a CNN with about 1,900 parameters reach 94.4% on digits?
options: The digits were so simple that any model would score that high.
It used a pretrained backbone from ImageNet.
The CNN memorised the test set during training.
Weight sharing reuses detectors everywhere.
questions.explanation: With fewer parameters than one fully connected layer would need for the raw pixels, the CNN works because its inductive bias fits images.

bookExercises.prompt: Define translation equivariance and translation invariance in one sentence each, and state which one convolution alone provides.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Translation equivariance: if the input shifts, the output shifts correspondingly. Translation invariance: the output doesn't change when the input shifts. Convolution alone provides equivariance; invariance requires pooling (or similar) applied afterward.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 68.1's formula, compute the output size of an 8x8 input through a 3x3 kernel with padding=0, stride=1, and explain why this differs from the "same"-padding case.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `(8 + 2*0 - 3) // 1 + 1 = 6`. This differs from the "same"-padding case (output 8) because no padding is added, so the kernel can't be centered on the border pixels. The output shrinks by `kernel_size - 1 = 2` pixels total (1 lost from each side) compared to same-padding, which pads exactly enough to keep the output the same size as the input.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's measured augmentation result (0.874 ± 0.016 without vs. 0.866 ± 0.013 with augmentation), explain why the overlapping error ranges (mean ± std) matter for concluding "augmentation didn't help" rather than "augmentation made it slightly worse."
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The two conditions' mean±std ranges (0.874 ± 0.016, i.e. roughly 0.858-0.890, and 0.866 ± 0.013, i.e. roughly 0.853-0.879) overlap substantially. The difference between the two means (0.008) is smaller than either individual standard deviation. This overlap means the observed difference is well within what random seed variation alone would produce, so "augmentation didn't help" (a null result) is the honest conclusion. Claiming "augmentation made it slightly worse" would be over-interpreting noise as a real, directional effect that the data doesn't actually support at this level of measurement precision.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's ~1,900-parameter CNN reaching 94.4% accuracy, explain in your own words why weight sharing is the specific mechanism that makes this parameter count sufficient, connecting it to Exposition's fully-connected-layer parameter-count comparison.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Weight sharing means the same small kernel (e.g. 9 weights for a 3x3 kernel) is applied at every spatial position in the image, rather than each position needing its own independent set of weights. A fully-connected layer processing the same image would need one weight per (input pixel, output unit) pair. The CNN instead reuses roughly 1,900 weights total across every position the kernels slide over, because the assumption "an edge looks the same regardless of where it appears" lets one learned detector serve the whole image instead of needing a separately-learned detector per position, which is exactly why ~1,900 parameters is enough to reach 94.4% accuracy where a comparably-sized fully-connected network would need vastly more.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague copies a standard ImageNet augmentation pipeline (flips, rotation, colour jitter) onto a medical X-ray classification task without modification. Using this chapter's Procedure 68.3 and Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say about what to check first.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Before assuming that pipeline helps, check whether flips make sense for X-rays specifically. Many anatomical structures have a canonical left/right orientation that a horizontal flip would violate, and colour jitter is largely meaningless for grayscale medical imagery. Beyond label-preservation, this chapter's own augmentation experiment showed that even a 'safe' augmentation's *strength* has to be calibrated to the image's actual scale and resolution. A default tuned for large natural photos measurably didn't help on much smaller images, so the pipeline needs to be measured on this specific dataset, not assumed to transfer."

bookExercises.prompt: A new CNN throws a shape-mismatch error on its first forward pass. Using Procedure 68.1's warning, describe the specific debugging step to take before assuming the error is in the model architecture itself.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Before assuming the bug is in the model architecture (wrong layer types, wrong activation choice, etc.), explicitly compute the expected output size through every conv/pool layer in sequence using the output-size formula, and compare that computed flatten dimension against what the first fully-connected layer was actually declared with. A shape-mismatch error is very often simply an arithmetic mistake in this calculation (e.g. forgetting a pooling layer halves the spatial size) rather than a deeper design flaw, and checking this first is much faster than debugging the architecture's logic.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about the vanishing-gradient problem as it affects very deep plain CNNs (referenced in this chapter's "Where This Hits a Wall"). Identify what specifically about stacking many convolutional layers (without skip connections) causes gradients to vanish, in your own words, before reading Chapter 69's solution.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: In a plain (no skip connections) deep CNN, the gradient of the loss with respect to an early layer's weights is computed via the chain rule as a product of many per-layer partial derivatives, one for each layer between that early layer and the output. If each of these per-layer factors is somewhat less than 1 (which is common with saturating activations or certain weight initialisations), multiplying many such factors together causes the product to shrink exponentially with depth, so by the time the gradient signal reaches the earliest layers, it has become vanishingly small, and those layers barely update during training despite technically receiving a gradient, effectively becoming untrainable once the network is deep enough.
